notes:
Now let me compile the notes. I have gathered substantial material from Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican), Ligonier (Reformed), and excerpts from GTY (Baptist/Calvinistic) and Desiring God (Reformed Baptist). Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Genesis 50 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: *"Then Joseph fell upon his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him."*

- **Traditional reading:** This tender scene shows Joseph's deep love for his father. His grief is expressed openly — weeping and kissing the dead was a natural, acceptable expression of mourning, as also seen in David and Christ. Joseph had been present for Jacob's final words and blessings and now says his farewell. (Gill notes the ancient practice among pagans of catching the departing soul with a kiss.) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The scene forms the conclusion of Jacob's death narrative (49:28–50:14) and sets up Joseph's final days. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers

---

### vv. 2–3: *"Joseph directed the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel… forty days… the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days."*

- **Traditional reading:** Embalming was necessary for the long journey to Canaan. Egypt was famous for its physicians, who were specialists (Herodotus notes a physician for each disease). Joseph used his household physicians to superintend the embalming. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Gill:** Describes the Egyptian embalming process in detail from Herodotus: brain extracted through nostrils, bowels removed through a flank incision, cavity filled with myrrh and cassia, body pickled in nitre for 70 days, then wrapped in linen. Gill says the 70 days of mourning may be a round number for the 72 days Diodorus Siculus records for a king, with two days deducted to show Jacob was not quite a king of Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

- **Ellicott:** Herodotus says embalming took 70 days, but that was at Thebes; at Memphis (Joseph's time) it took about 40 days. Diodorus agrees: embalming took somewhat more than 30 days, royal mourning 72 days. The 40 days of embalming were probably included in the 70 days of mourning. Normal Israelite mourning was 30 days (Num 20:29; Deut 34:8). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Jacob was mourned 70 days by the whole nation — a royal-level honour (royal mourning in Egypt was 72 days). Jacob was greatly honoured. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

---

### vv. 4–5: *"When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph said to Pharaoh's court…"*

- **Why Joseph spoke through intermediaries:** Several views appear across the commentaries:
  - **Ellicott:** No one in mourning attire could enter the royal presence (cf. Esther 4:2); a mourner's dress was squalid, beard unshorn, hair disordered. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm
  - **Gill:** Either Joseph was at a distance in Goshen and sent a messenger, or these were courtiers who had come to condole with him; or it was a Persian-like custom that mourners could not appear before the king. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm
  - **Pulpit Commentary (via StudyLight):** Several theories: (a) Joseph could not appear before Pharaoh in mourning (Rosenmüller); (b) he wished to maintain good relations with the priesthood who handled burial matters (Havernick); (c) most likely, Joseph had let his beard and hair grow according to Egyptian custom and could not enter the king's presence without being shaven and shorn (Hengstenberg, Kurtz, Keil). The Pulpit Commentary rejects the theory that Joseph's power was restricted after the famine. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-50.html
  - **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This small, authentic detail — approaching through the household rather than directly — is exactly the sort of thing a true eyewitness would record, not something a storyteller would invent. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **"The tomb that I dug for myself":** The Hebrew verb can mean "dug" or "bought" (Onkelos renders it "bought"). Jacob may have enlarged the cave at Machpelah or prepared a specific niche for himself. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-50.html

- **Joseph's promise to return:** Gill notes Joseph specifically says "I will come again" to assure Pharaoh this was not an excuse to flee Egypt with his wealth. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

---

### v. 6: *"Pharaoh replied, 'Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.'"*

- **Traditional reading:** Gill observes that the oath seems to be the principal thing influencing Pharaoh — oaths were regarded as sacred and inviolable. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

---

### vv. 7–9: *"all the servants of Pharaoh… elders… chariots and horsemen… an exceedingly large procession."*

- **Traditional reading:** This was an extraordinary state funeral. The Hebrew word for "company" (v.9) is *camp* — suggesting military escort as well as honour. The presence of chariots and horsemen served both grandeur and security against possible attack by robbers or Canaanite resistance. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Luther remarked that no burial in Scripture is recorded with such honour or such wealth of detail. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Only the little ones and flocks left in Goshen:** This demonstrated they fully intended to return to Egypt — not using the funeral as a pretext to escape. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

---

### vv. 10–11: *"the threshing floor of Atad, which is across the Jordan… lamented and wailed loudly… seven days… Abel-mizraim."*

- **Location debate:** Ellicott discusses whether "beyond Jordan" means east or west. He argues the route lay east of the Dead Sea, through Moab and Ammon, because the western route through the wilderness of Judah was too difficult for chariots, and the Philistine route may have been hostile. Jerome placed Goren-Atad at Beth-Hoglah, between the Jordan and Jericho. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Abel-mizraim — a wordplay:** Ellicott notes the Hebrew text as pointed reads *Abel-mizraim* ("meadow of Egypt"), but the word for "mourning" is *êbel*. The ancient versions (LXX, etc.) all read *Ebel-mizraim* ("mourning of Egypt"). The Canaanites mistook the entire company for Egyptians because of the Egyptian-dominated procession. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Seven days of mourning:** This became the standard Israelite mourning period (cf. 1 Sam 31:13). Joseph observed this either at the threshing floor or after the burial itself. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

---

### vv. 12–13: *"Jacob's sons did as he had charged them. They carried him… and buried him in the cave at Machpelah…"*

- **Traditional reading:** All the sons — not only Joseph — obeyed Jacob's command. The cave of Machpelah was the only piece of Canaan to which Abraham held a legal title deed (Gen 23). It was the burial place of Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah. Jacob's sons who had often disappointed him in life honoured him in death. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

---

### v. 14: *"After Joseph had buried his father, he returned to Egypt…"*

- **Traditional reading:** Joseph kept his word to Pharaoh. The brothers also returned, having left their families and flocks as surety. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm

---

### v. 15: *"When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, 'What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us…'"*

- **Traditional reading:** The brothers' guilty consciences resurfaced after Jacob's death. They feared Joseph had only restrained himself for Jacob's sake. Gill notes their sin "came fresh to their remembrance, guilt arose in their consciences and flew in their faces." This was the pattern of Esau, who vowed to wait until Isaac died before taking revenge (Gen 27:41). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/50.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Matthew Henry is quoted: "A guilty conscience exposes men to continual fright. Those who would be fearless must keep themselves guiltless." The brothers' fear is remarkable given that Joseph had already voiced his pardon and provided for them (Gen 45:1–47:12). Guilt makes us ashamed to face those we have offended until we confess. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers

---

### vv. 16–17: *"So they sent word to Joseph, saying, 'Before he died, your father commanded… I beg you, please forgive the transgression…'"*

- **Was the message fabricated?** Most conservative commentators believe the brothers' story was probably made up:
  - **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "This story was probably made up. They didn't feel they had the moral right to ask Joseph for mercy… so they put the request for mercy in the mouth of their honoured and dead father." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/
  - **Ligonier/Reformed:** "Men often lie when they are afraid, and Joseph's brothers may have bended the truth… This was entirely unnecessary, their brother was not a vindictive man." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers
  - **Ellicott (more cautious):** Many Jewish expositors consider this untrue, and that Jacob was never aware they sold Joseph. However, Gen 49:6 may indicate Jacob knew and saw Simeon and Levi as chief offenders. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **The brothers' confession was genuine:** Ligonier notes they used three of the four chief Hebrew terms for iniquity: "transgression" (*pesha*), "sin" (*chattat*), and "evil" (*ra'ah*). They also invoked "the God of your father," implicitly asking Joseph to imitate God's forgiving nature (Ps 130:4). — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers

- **Joseph wept:** Guzik says Joseph wept because his brothers "thought so little of him, and they doubted his character so greatly." Ligonier says he wept "probably because his brothers had not yet received his love." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers

---

### v. 18: *"His brothers also came to him, bowed down before him, and said, 'We are your slaves!'"*

- **Traditional reading:** The brothers' bowing fulfills Joseph's boyhood dreams (Gen 37). They offer themselves as slaves — the very condition into which they had sold Joseph. Their humility was genuine, driven by fear. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/ ; https://www.gty.org/sermons/print/80-388/joseph-because-god-meant-it-for-good

---

### vv. 19–20: *"'Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good…'"*

This is the theological summit of Genesis, and Protestant traditions largely agree on its meaning, though with differing emphases:

#### Traditional / Common Reading

- **"Am I in the place of God?"** — Joseph understood that vengeance belongs to God alone (cf. Rom 12:19). Judges in Hebrew are sometimes called *elohim* (Ex 21:6; 22:8–9) as exercising God's authority. Joseph refuses that role. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **"You meant evil… God meant it for good"** — The same Hebrew verb (*chashab*) is used for both human and divine "intending." Joseph does not minimise his brothers' sin ("you meant evil"), but he sees a greater reality: God's sovereign purpose overruling it for good. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Calvin (Reformed):** Calvin rejects interpretations that Joseph was merely refusing worship or refusing personal vengeance. He sees Joseph acknowledging that "the whole affair was conducted by the counsel of God, and not by his own." Calvin says this passage also teaches that Joseph's burial instructions were a "seal of redemption" — the bones were "useful relics" signifying that God's eternal covenant had not become extinct. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-50.html

#### Reformed / Calvinistic Emphasis

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** Insists the verse does NOT say "God *used* it for good" but "God *meant* it for good." The same verb for "meant/intended" governs both clauses, and "it" refers to the same event (Joseph being sold). God did not merely react to the brothers' sin — He planned it, predicted it in a dream, superintended it for 22 years, and brought about deliverance through it. "God is not surprised by the sins of his people and then scratches his head about how to 'use' it for good." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/does-god-intend-evil-for-our-good

- **John MacArthur (GTY / Baptist, Calvinistic):** This is the doctrine of providence — "God works His own ends. No matter what the intention of people, be it good or bad, God will bring about His own ultimate end." Joseph's theology of God's sovereignty "generated the attitude of his heart." God's plan was vast: preserve the family → form a nation → bring the Messiah → save the world. — https://www.gty.org/sermons/print/80-388/joseph-because-god-meant-it-for-good

- **Sinclair Ferguson (Monergism / Reformed):** Preached a sermon titled "God Meant It for Good" on this passage, emphasising that after all, Joseph's dreams came true — his brothers bowed before him as servants — yet Joseph's response was grace, not vengeance. — https://www.monergism.com/god-meant-it-good-genesis-50

#### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik)

- Emphasis on the **chain of providence**: if the brothers never sell Joseph → he never reaches Egypt → never interprets Pharaoh's dream → never becomes prime minister → family perishes in famine → Messiah never comes → all humanity remains dead in sin. The "liberating truth is that ultimately, our lives are not in the hands of men, but in the hands of God." Guzik adds the illustration of the silk bookmark — tangled and meaningless on the back, "God is love" on the front. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

#### Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)

- Joseph recognised his life as "a Divine thing." He was "only an instrument in the hands of God, in the place of God. He saw Providence working with grace." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/genesis/50.htm

---

### v. 21: *"Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones." So Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them."*

- **Traditional reading:** Joseph's forgiveness was not just words — it was backed by practical provision. He "comforted them and spoke kindly to them" (literally "spoke to their heart"). The "little ones" (*taf*) refers to their dependents and households. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** This is the fruit of trusting God rather than oneself to repay transgressors (Prov 20:22). Calvin is cited: "if we have an arduous conflict with the impetuosity of an angry temper… we must pray to the Lord for a spirit of meekness." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joseph-and-his-brothers

---

### vv. 22–23: *"Joseph… lived to the age of 110. He saw Ephraim's sons to the third generation, and indeed the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph's knees."*

- **Traditional reading:** 110 was considered the ideal Egyptian lifespan. Seeing great-grandchildren (Ephraim's "third generation," e.g. Eran son of Shuthelah son of Ephraim, Num 26:35–36) was evidence of God's blessing on Joseph's long life despite his early hardships. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **"Brought up on Joseph's knees":** The Hebrew literally says "were born upon Joseph's knees" — meaning they were adopted by him or acknowledged as his own (cf. Gen 30:3). They would count as Joseph's children, forming "families" though not tribes. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

---

### v. 24: *"Then Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.'"*

- **Traditional reading:** Joseph's last words are a confession of faith. Though he was the human agent who brought Israel to Egypt, he knew Egypt was not their home. He trusted God's covenant promise. Ellicott: "This is, first, a proof of Joseph's faith, commended in Hebrews 11:22; and, secondly, it is a preparation for the next book (Exodus). Joseph's faith thus unites the two books together." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Calvin:** Joseph's faith rested on God's faithfulness — "he deems it sufficient to adduce the oath of God, to remove all their doubts respecting their deliverance." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-50.html

---

### vv. 25–26: *"Joseph made the sons of Israel take an oath… 'God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.' So Joseph died at the age of 110… they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt."*

- **Traditional reading:** Joseph was never buried in Egypt. His coffin (a wooden mummy-case, typically sycamore wood) lay above ground for roughly 400 years as a silent witness. Whenever a child of Israel asked why that coffin remained unburied, the answer was: "Because Joseph did not want to be buried in Egypt, but in the Promised Land God will one day lead us to." The promise was fulfilled at the Exodus (Ex 13:19) and the burial at Shechem (Josh 24:32). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

- **Hebrews 11:22:** The New Testament singles out this act — not Joseph's governance of Egypt, not his interpretation of dreams, but his dying instructions about his bones — as the great example of his faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Calvin:** Joseph's bones were "useful relics, the sight of which plainly signified that, by the death of men, the eternal covenant in which Joseph commands his posterity safely to rest, had by no means become extinct." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-50.html

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The Book of Genesis — the Book of Beginnings — ends looking forward to God's unfolding plan of redemption. It concludes "looking forward to the continuation of God's eternal, loving, wise plan." Guzik illustrates with George Mueller, who prayed 20,000 times over 11 years for one request: "Go on waiting upon God, go on praying." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-50/

- **Why not buried immediately?** Ellicott: After Joseph's death, the Israelites no longer had a military escort to travel to Hebron, so his embalmed body was kept accessible in Goshen for the future Exodus. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/50.htm

---

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Traditional Emphases on Key Verses

| Tradition | Emphasis on vv. 19–20 | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Reformed** (Calvin, Ligonier, Ferguson) | God's sovereign counsel ordained the evil for good; Joseph's refusal of vengeance flows from trusting God's providence | Ligonier, Calvin, Monergism |
| **Reformed Baptist / Desiring God** (John Piper) | God did not merely *use* the evil — He *meant* it, planned it. The same Hebrew verb governs both clauses. This is the foundation for Romans 8:28 | desiringgod.org |
| **Baptist / GTY** (John MacArthur) | God's providence coordinates all independent human actions toward His ultimate end; Joseph's theology of sovereignty generated his forgiving attitude | gty.org |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (David Guzik) | Emphasis on the "chain of providence" — each link necessary for Messiah's coming; practical application: freedom from bitterness comes from trusting God's overruling hand | enduringword.com |
| **Older Anglican** (Ellicott) | Focus on lexical detail (the same Hebrew verb for "meant"), and the verse as showing God's purpose contrasting man's purpose | biblehub.com/ellicott |
| **Older Baptist** (Gill) | Detailed historical background on Egyptian customs; the brothers' fear as a guilty conscience; Joseph's kindness as exemplary | biblehub.com/gill |

**Limitations of this research:** I was unable to retrieve dedicated pages from Methodist/Wesleyan sources (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org), Catholic sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox sources (oca.org), or modern critical scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) within the available searches. The Pulpit Commentary, Calvin's Commentary, and Gray's Concise Commentary were found via StudyLight but could not be fully fetched. Where these sources are cited above, the content comes from search result excerpts rather than full-page retrievals.
